how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Siding bid calculator

How much should I charge for vinyl siding?

Enough to cover the squares you will actually hang, not enough to match the cheapest postcard on the block. A one-story vinyl wrap with four windows and a two-story fiber-cement tear-off with gables are not the same job, and a flat price per square foot cannot see the difference.

Open the free bid calculator

Price the net wall, then the waste

Start with length × height on each elevation. Subtract openings once — windows and doors are not siding. Convert the remainder to squares (100 sq ft) and add waste. Vinyl often needs about 10%; fiber cement and engineered wood run higher because of cuts and breakage. That waste is material you buy and hours you spend. Leaving it out is how a “measured” bid still comes up a square short.

Height, tear-off, and openings are not “included”

A ranch is the install you already priced. A second story is not twice the hours, but it is not the same hours either — staging, carrying, and ladder time add a real fraction. Tear-off is its own hours plus a dumpster. Each window and door is wrap and J-channel, not a hole that makes the job cheaper. If those lines are “included” in an $8-a-foot special, they are unpaid.

Linear trim is a second materials list

Starter, outside corners, inside corners, J-channel, and undersill are priced by the foot, not by the square. A small house with many openings can spend as much on trim as on an extra square of siding. Contractors who quote only the field and “figure trim in” are guessing the line that most often blows the takeoff.

Then load the wage and keep a margin

An installer paid $32 often costs more than $42 once employer taxes, ladder-and-tear-off workers’ compensation, liability, and paid time off are counted. Overhead sits on top of that direct cost. Margin is a share of the price the customer sees, not a markup you add last and forget. The walk-away number is total cost: below it the job makes nothing, even before you pay yourself.

This is not a manufacturer price list

This is not a manufacturer price list, not a building-code requirement, and not a finding that a wall is weathertight or due for replacement. The starting hours and material figures are ballpark numbers so a contractor can see the shape of a bid. Replace them with times and invoices from your own jobs, confirm measurements on site, and have a qualified professional review anything that has to be signed or insured.

Price this job in the calculator

Common questions

How much should I charge for vinyl siding?

Charge the hours and material the job will actually take — net wall area plus waste, times stories, plus tear-off, housewrap, openings, linear trim, travel, and a dumpster — then divide cost by one minus your target margin. A flat price per square foot hides the difference between a one-story vinyl wrap and a two-story fiber-cement tear-off.

Why do two houses of the same size bid so differently?

Waste, height, openings, and tear-off. A gable elevation is not a ranch wall, and twelve windows are not four. A neighborhood special that ignores those lines is how a crew works a week for a three-day price.

Is this a manufacturer price list?

No. Starting hours and material figures are editable ballpark numbers, not a manufacturer price list, a code table, or a finding that any wall is weathertight or due for replacement. Confirm measurements on site.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a manufacturer, building-code, or insurance inspection. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

FOR SIDING CONTRACTORS

Bid the squares and the waste, not the house.

A one-story vinyl wrap with four windows is not the same job as a two-story fiber-cement tear-off with gables. Price the net wall, the waste, the height, the openings, and the linear trim — then see the walk-away number before a price-per-square-foot special eats the week.

How much should I charge for vinyl siding? · this calculator vs. JobNimbus · this calculator vs. a flat rate per square.

The walls

One row per elevation. Length × height is the gross wall. Openings come off the total below — do not pre-subtract them here or you will double-count.

ElevationLength (ft)Height (ft)

The job

A square is 100 sq ft of wall. Waste covers cuts, starter, and damaged pieces — vinyl often needs about 10%, fiber cement more. Stories multiply install hours. None of this is a manufacturer table or a weathertightness finding — it is a time and material budget you can edit.

Linear trim

Trim is where a price-per-square-foot bid goes quiet. A small house with many windows can spend as much on J-channel and corners as on a whole extra square of siding.

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation (ladders and tear-off are not cheap), liability insurance, and paid time off. An installer paid $32 often costs more than $42 on the wall. Underestimating that is how an $8-a-foot special loses money.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the homeowner — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Where the wall area goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting hours and material figures are common ballpark numbers, not a manufacturer price list, a code table, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them. This is not a finding that any wall is weathertight, permitted, or due for replacement.

    Common questions

    How do I work out how many squares of siding a house needs?

    Enter each elevation as a length × height row. The calculator adds them into gross wall area, subtracts the window and door area you enter, divides the remainder by 100 to get net squares, then adds waste to get the billable squares that material and install hours are priced from. Waste starts at 10% for vinyl and aluminum and 12% for fiber cement and engineered wood — those are common starting points, not a manufacturer allowance, and a cut-up elevation with lots of gables needs more.

    If I subtract the windows, why is there still a charge per opening?

    Because the two are different costs. Subtracting opening square footage stops you buying siding for glass. Cutting and fitting around that opening is a labor line of its own — about 0.35 h per opening here — and the J-channel or window wrap around it is priced separately by the linear foot. A wall with fourteen windows and a wall with two can have the same net square footage and are nowhere near the same day's work; a per-square-foot quote cannot tell them apart.

    How much does a second or third storey add?

    Install hours are multiplied by 1.0 for one storey, 1.35 for two, and 1.7 for three or more. That multiplier is height and staging — carrying material up, moving pump jacks, working off a plank — not "a bigger house", so it applies to install hours only and not to tear-off, housewrap, trim, or the flat add-ons. Scaffold or pump jacks are their own add-on line with hours and rental cost, because that is a job-level decision rather than something that scales with area.

    Does tear-off cost the same as installing?

    No, it is its own hours-per-square figure, and the presets put it at roughly a third to a half of install: about 2.0 h/square against 4.5 for vinyl, 2.5 against 7.0 for fiber cement. Tear-off also brings the dumpster, which is a separate flat cost, and it is optional — a siding-over job turns tear-off hours off entirely while keeping housewrap, which is priced from net squares rather than billable squares because wrap does not need the cut waste.

    Why does a small siding repair still price at more than the material?

    Round-trip drive time comes from the miles and speed you enter, setup is its own line, and a minimum on-site hours floor applies when the takeoff comes in under it — a crew that mobilizes has those hours gone whether the wall is four squares or forty. The trip or truck fee sits on top as a flat line. Making the floor visible is the point: it is what a "just a couple of panels" call actually costs you.

    Why isn't a 20% margin the same as adding 20% to my cost?

    Margin here is a share of the final price — price = job cost ÷ (1 − margin) — which is how the quote reads to the homeowner and how your books read it. Overhead is a separate markup on the job's direct cost, applied before margin and never to itself or to profit. A $14,000 cost marked up 20% is $16,800, a 16.7% margin; a 20% target margin is $17,500. vs-a-flat-rate-per-square.html.text:
← Siding Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square

“$X a square, any siding job” is a price for one story count, one material, and one tear-off situation, quietly applied to a taller house with heavier material and old siding to strip that the flat number never carried.

What a flat rate per square is

A flat rate per square (100 square feet of wall) is the fastest way to quote a siding job over the phone: multiply the billable squares by a number and read it back. Homeowners like it because it is easy to compare against a competitor's quote, and it is the number a customer holding one will ask you to match.

The number behind it was usually set for the simplest version of the job — a one-story vinyl re-side over sound existing siding, with no tear-off and light trim — and then reused for every job afterward, whether or not the next one is two or three stories, heavier material, a full tear-off with a dumpster, or an elevation set with far more trim and openings.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each wall's length and height, openings, waste, material, stories, whether the job needs tear-off and housewrap, trim by the linear foot, and any add-ons, plus your own wage, payroll burden, material costs, overhead, and target margin. It prices siding material and install labor from the actual billable squares and story multiplier, tear-off and housewrap as their own lines only when the job needs them, openings by count, and trim by the linear foot — for this job, not a flat rate for every job.

What a flat rate per square doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same per square whether the house is one story or three, even though a taller wall needs more staging and reach per square installed. Multiplies install labor by a story factor — 1.35× for two stories, 1.7× for three — from the actual story count, not a single height for every job.
Has no line for tear-off or a dumpster, even though stripping old siding and hauling it away is real labor and a real disposal cost a re-side over sound siding never needs. Prices tear-off labor and a dumpster as their own line, only when the job needs them.
Has no line for housewrap, even though wrapping the house before the new siding goes up is priced by net wall area and is not always part of the job. Prices housewrap from the actual net wall square footage, only when the job includes it.
Has no line for opening count, even though each window and door adds real labor to trim out regardless of house size. Prices opening labor from the actual count of windows and doors.
Has no line for starter strip, corners, J-channel, or undersill trim, even though trim is priced by the linear foot and does not track wall area. Prices each trim item from its own linear footage, separate from the siding itself.

Two houses, one flat rate

Using this calculator's own figures, at a 28% target margin, a $32 hourly wage, and 34% payroll burden:

A one-story vinyl wrap with no tear-off costs $4,892.04 to run and this calculator prices it at $6,794.49 for 8.91 billable squares — $762.57 per square. A two-story fiber-cement tear-off with housewrap and heavier trim costs $22,874.89 to run and this calculator prices it at $31,770.68 for 19.31 billable squares, 4.68 times the vinyl job's price on just 2.17 times the squares. Quote the fiber-cement job at the vinyl job's flat $762.57-per-square rate instead, and 19.31 squares prices at $14,724.30 — $8,150.59 short of the $22,874.89 it costs to build. The flat rate does not just erode the margin here: it prices the job at a loss before it ever clears its own cost.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square get a bigger siding job wrong?

Because almost nothing in a siding job scales with squares alone. A second or third story multiplies install labor for staging and reach, not material. Tear-off adds a labor line and a dumpster that a re-side over existing siding never needs. Housewrap is priced by net wall area, not billable squares. Openings add labor per window and door regardless of house size, and trim -- starter strip, corners, J-channel, undersill -- is priced by linear feet, which does not track wall area the way a flat per-square rate assumes. A rate set on a simple one-story vinyl wrap carries none of that, because a simple one-story job does not have it to carry.

What does a flat per-square rate usually leave out entirely?

Story height, tear-off and dumpster, housewrap, opening count, and linear trim. A flat per-square number has no line for the extra staging and reach a second or third story adds to install labor, no line for stripping old siding and hauling it away, no line for wrapping the house before the new siding goes up, no line for the labor each window and door opening adds regardless of house size, and no line for corners, starter strip, J-channel, and undersill trim priced by the linear foot.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own figures at a $32 hourly wage, 34% payroll burden, and a 28% target margin: a one-story vinyl wrap with no tear-off costs $4,892.04 to run and this calculator prices it at $6,794.49 for 8.91 billable squares -- $762.57 per square. A two-story fiber-cement tear-off with housewrap costs $22,874.89 to run and this calculator prices it at $31,770.68 for 19.31 billable squares, 4.68 times the vinyl job's price on just 2.17 times the squares. Quote the fiber-cement job at the vinyl job's flat $762.57-per-square rate instead, and 19.31 squares prices at $14,724.30 -- $8,150.59 short of the $22,874.89 it costs to build.

Is a flat rate per square ever the right way to quote?

For a job close to the story count, material, and tear-off situation the rate was set on -- typically a one-story vinyl re-side with no tear-off and light trim -- a flat per-square number can land close, because that is probably the job the rate was set on. The risk is quoting a taller house, a heavier material, a tear-off, or a trim-heavy elevation set at the same rate, because the rate does not know the stories, the material, or whether the old siding comes off until someone measures the walls, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted over the phone.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your supplier's material pricing, or what other siding contractors in your area charge. It takes per-elevation wall measurements, waste, material, stories, openings, tear-off, housewrap, and trim you supply, plus your own wage, burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat rate per square skips, not a market survey.

Open the Siding Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read how much should I charge for vinyl siding.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge or whether a wall may be resided. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and supply costs, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device: it is a static page that runs the same arithmetic you can check in the calculator itself.

Free and open source. If it wins you a job, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-jobnimbus.html.text:
← Siding Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. JobNimbus

Two different shapes: JobNimbus is an account-based CRM and job management platform for running an exterior contractor's whole lead-to-job pipeline. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one siding job cost, given its walls, waste, openings, and tear-off, before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

JobNimbus is a CRM and job management platform, founded in 2013 by Ben Hodson, Nick Wood, and Jason Wood, headquartered in Lehi, Utah. It is built for roofing, siding, gutter, solar, and other exterior contractors, covering lead and pipeline tracking, estimates and proposals, scheduling, job costing, and invoicing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. JobNimbus's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a CRM and job management platform serving exterior trades including siding, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for JobNimbus appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what JobNimbus does. It does not track a lead, schedule a crew, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one job's wall area by elevation, openings, stories, and material (vinyl, fiber cement, engineered wood, or aluminum), with waste, tear-off, housewrap, linear trim, scaffold, and soffit/fascia as their own line items, plus loaded installer wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price, the price per billable square and per net square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run a siding company and need leads, estimates, scheduling, and invoicing tracked in one system across every crew and every job.JobNimbus, or a comparable CRM — running the whole pipeline is not something this calculator does.
What should I charge for this siding job, given its walls, waste, openings, stories, and extras?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
How much does a two-story fiber-cement tear-off with fourteen openings actually add over a one-story vinyl wrap?This calculator's material, story, opening, and tear-off split, not a flat price per square foot.
Is the price I'm about to quote still above my walk-away cost for this job?This calculator's compare-to-proposed-price check.
I need my whole sales and install team working the same leads and paperwork from one shared account.JobNimbus — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a siding bid actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. JobNimbus is used through a subscription account.

Most siding contractors get different value from each: JobNimbus (or a comparable CRM) for running the company's whole lead-to-job pipeline and paperwork as an ongoing subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one siding job should cost from its walls, waste, and extras before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a lead record, a scheduled job, or a signed contract.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or JobNimbus?

They do different jobs, and a siding company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. JobNimbus, founded in 2013 by Ben Hodson, Nick Wood, and Jason Wood and headquartered in Lehi, Utah, is a CRM and job management platform built for roofing, siding, gutter, and other exterior contractors, covering lead tracking, estimates, scheduling, and invoicing across a whole business, sold as an ongoing subscription account. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from per-elevation wall measurements, waste, stories, openings, and tear-off, with linear trim, housewrap, dumpster, and add-ons as their own line items, plus loaded installer wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin, it turns that into the price, the price per billable square, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, before any of it touches a business-management system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A siding company that already tracks leads, schedules crews, and invoices across every job is better served by JobNimbus or a comparable CRM; a contractor who wants an instant, private answer to what one siding job should cost from its walls, waste, and extras before opening a business system is in the right place here.
